concepts.title: Computer vision as a scientific quest
concepts.one_liner: Computer vision is an interdisciplinary scientific quest focused on understanding how natural intelligence and perception works.
concepts.content: Computer vision has become an exciting and fast-evolving area of research. It is important to understand the field within the scientific context of broader inquiry. Computer vision is not just an engineering discipline that tries to build systems that see; instead, it is another aspect of the interdisciplinary scientific quest focused on understanding how natural intelligence and perception works.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept frames computer vision not merely as a tool for building machines, but as a fundamental scientific endeavor to decode the principles of biological perception.
concepts.recap_md: - Computer vision is an interdisciplinary field beyond simple engineering.

concepts.title: Learning-based vs model-based vision
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based approaches rely on flexible architectures and data to build models for perception rather than starting with fixed hypotheses.
concepts.content: While many previous perspectives on perception began with models about how perception might work, learning-based approaches take a different path. They rely on flexible architectures that incorporate as few hypotheses about perception as possible, and instead focus on data to learn to build the right model for perception.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional model-based approaches often fail when the underlying assumptions are wrong; learning-based methods allow the system to discover the structure of perception directly from data.

concepts.title: Empiricism vs rationalism in vision
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision is rooted in empiricism, the philosophical tradition holding that knowledge is acquired through experience and data.
concepts.content: Learning-based vision has its roots in the philosophical tradition of empiricism, which holds that knowledge about the world should be acquired by experience, rather than solely through reason (an approach known as rationalism). The modern-day term for experience is "data," and learning is really all about data.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the philosophical roots of vision helps distinguish between systems built on human logic (rationalism) and those built on observed evidence (empiricism).

concepts.title: Programming vs learning algorithms
concepts.one_liner: Learning derives vision algorithms by fitting functions to data rather than writing explicit code or deriving rules from world models.
concepts.content: Learning derives vision algorithms by fitting functions to data. There are a few ways to "program" a vision algorithm (@fig-taxonomy-programming_vs_learning). One way is to write the algorithm directly in Python code, such as comparing pixel intensities and setting thresholds. Another approach is to derive the algorithm as the rational thing to do given an underlying model of the world; for example, detecting boundaries by looking for contrast edges produced by overlapping objects. The third approach—the learning approach—is to program algorithms via data: first collect examples of inputs and correct outputs, then fit a function that replicates these mappings.
concepts.motivation_md: Explicitly programming every visual rule is often impossible due to the complexity of the real world; learning from data provides a scalable alternative.
concepts.recap_md: - Algorithms can be written directly, derived from models, or learned from data.

key_passage.text: One way is to write the algorithm directly in Python code: first we will compare the intensity of this pixel and that pixel, then we will threshold about some such value, and so on. Another approach is to derive the algorithm as the rational thing to do given some underlying model of the world, for example, because overlapping objects generically produce contrast edges in the image, the optimal way to detect boundaries between objects is to look for such and such particular kind of contrast. The third approach --- the learning approach --- is to program algorithms via data: first collect a bunch of examples of inputs and the correct output, then fit a function that replicates these exemplar mappings from input to output.

concepts.title: Perceptron learning algorithm
concepts.one_liner: The perceptron is a formal learning algorithm and early artificial neural net capable of recognizing simple visual patterns.
concepts.content: Learning algorithms have been a part of computer vision since the field's origins. In 1958, Frank Rosenblatt published one of the first formal learning algorithms, called the **perceptron** learning algorithm, and showed that it can, in principle, learn to recognize certain simple visual patterns. The perceptron was also one of the first artificial neural nets, a computational model of biological brains. The ability of perceptrons to learn to solve recognition problems created an explosion of interest in neural nets. Rosenblatt published the algorithm in the journal Psychological Review, illustrating the interdisciplinary nature of early AI.
concepts.motivation_md: The perceptron was the first attempt to model biological intelligence computationally to solve pattern recognition tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - The perceptron was one of the first formal learning algorithms and artificial neural nets.

concepts.title: Cycles of interest in neural networks
concepts.one_liner: Interest in neural networks has fluctuated over time, notably declining after proofs showed the limitations of simple perceptrons.
concepts.content: Interest in neural nets has gone through a series of ebbs and flows (@fig-taxonomy-neural_net_enthusiam). These cycles have partially lined up with interest in learning algorithms generally, though there were phases where interest in neural nets was low while other learning algorithms remained popular. In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published *Perceptrons: an introduction to computational geometry*. Although it was an introduction, the book largely killed excitement by showing that perceptrons are incapable of learning basic logical operations, leading to the conclusion that they could not be the basis of intelligence.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the history of AI helps researchers recognize that current trends are part of longer cycles of optimism and skepticism.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural network popularity has historically moved in cycles of roughly 25 years.

concepts.title: Deep learning
concepts.one_liner: Deep learning systems are modern neural networks built by stacking perceptrons to perform complex operations.
concepts.content: It wasn't until the 1980s that interest in learning algorithms, and neural nets in particular, began to surge again. The reason was because researchers showed that perceptrons could be stacked to create systems capable of complex operations, including logic. These systems were the precursors to the **deep learning** systems that are dominant today.
concepts.motivation_md: Deep learning overcomes the limitations of simple perceptrons by using multiple layers to represent complex hierarchical information.
concepts.recap_md: - Deep learning evolved from stacking perceptrons to handle complex logic.

concepts.title: Law of closure
concepts.one_liner: When a line forms a closed figure, we do not simply see a line, we see a shape.
concepts.content: The Law of closure describes the fact that when a line forms a closed figure, we do not simply see a line, but rather a shape. This principle can even override proximity cues; for example, vertical lines that are physically closer to one another may still be grouped into separate shapes if the spatial arrangement suggests closed figures.
concepts.motivation_md: This law explains how the visual system prioritizes the perception of complete objects and shapes over fragmented or disconnected lines.
concepts.recap_md:
- Closed figures are perceived as unified shapes rather than individual lines.
 - The tendency toward closure can override other grouping cues like proximity.

concepts.title: Law of good continuation
concepts.one_liner: Lines that follow each other pointing in the same direction are likely to be grouped together.
concepts.content:
The Law of good continuation states that edges are likely to be smooth. Lines that follow each other pointing in the same direction are likely to be grouped together. For instance, an X-shape is perceived as two lines that cross each other instead of perceiving it as a V-shape on top of an inverted V.

concepts.one_liner: Parallelism and symmetry act as grouping cues that induce clustering between visual elements.

concepts.title: Common fate
concepts.one_liner: When two elements have a common motion, they tend to group together.
concepts.content: Common fate is a very important grouping cue based on motion. When two elements share a common motion—such as the same acceleration, direction, or rate of change—they tend to be perceived as a group.
concepts.motivation_md: Motion is a powerful indicator that separate elements belong to the same object, helping us track moving entities in a dynamic environment.
concepts.recap_md:
- Elements moving in the same direction at the same speed are grouped together.
 - Common motion (fate) is a primary cue for perceptual organization in dynamic scenes.

concepts.title: Lightness perception
concepts.one_liner: Lightness is the visual system's attempt to extract reflectance based on the luminances in the scene.
concepts.content: Lightness is a perceptual quantity influenced by both the perceived reflectance and the perceived illumination of a surface. Adelson defines lightness as "the visual system's attempt to extract reflectance based on the luminances in the scene."
concepts.motivation_md: The visual system must distinguish between the inherent color of an object (reflectance) and the light falling on it (illumination) to perceive the world accurately.
concepts.recap_md:
- Lightness is a perceptual measure, not just a physical one.
 - It depends on the interaction between surface reflectance and environmental illumination.

concepts.title: Koffka ring illusion
concepts.one_liner: The Koffka ring is an illusion illustrating how perceptual grouping and context influence lightness perception.
concepts.content: The Koffka ring is an illusion introduced by Kurt Koffka to illustrate the power of perceptual grouping in lightness perception. In this display, a ring of uniform gray is shown. Depending on the spatial configuration, the lightness of the ring's two sides can appear very different, even though they have the same gray level. For example, splitting the ring into two halves with white space makes the sides look different. This experiment demonstrates that lightness perception is not a local process but involves considering the context and principles of grouping.
concepts.motivation_md: This illusion proves that our perception of an object's brightness is not just determined by the light hitting a single point on the retina, but by the surrounding context.
concepts.recap_md:
- Identical gray levels can appear different based on spatial configuration.
 - Lightness perception is a global process influenced by grouping and context.

concepts.title: Amodal completion
concepts.one_liner: Amodal completion is the phenomenon of perceiving a whole object when only a part is visible.
concepts.content: Amodal completion is the visual phenomenon of perceiving a whole object even when it is partially occluded. For example, if a red square is placed on top of a blue square, we still see the blue shape as a complete square despite the occlusion. If a gap is introduced that breaks the illusion of occlusion, the perception of the whole object is lost. The term "amodal" refers to perception occurring without direct perceptual modality for the hidden parts. This is a process we use constantly to extend objects behind occlusions in everyday scenes.
concepts.motivation_md: Because most objects in the real world are partially hidden by other objects, amodal completion allows us to maintain a stable perception of whole entities.
concepts.recap_md:
- We perceive complete objects even when parts are hidden by occluders.
 - This process is essential for navigating and understanding 3D environments.

concepts.title: Backpropagation
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation is an efficient method for training neural networks, famously demonstrated by Yann LeCun et al. in 1989 for handwritten digit recognition.
concepts.content: In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. showed how neural networks can be efficiently trained using backpropagation. Their system was successfully put into practical use by the US Postal Service for the task of recognizing handwritten digits.
concepts.motivation_md: Backpropagation was developed to provide a computationally efficient way to train multi-layer neural networks, moving them from theoretical models to practical tools for pattern recognition.

concepts.title: Boosting
concepts.one_liner: Boosting is a simple learning algorithm used to create efficient and high-performing detectors, such as the Viola-Jones face detector.
concepts.content: In 2001, Paul Viola and Michael Jones published a method that used a simple learning algorithm called boosting to detect faces in photos. This method outperformed the complicated hand-engineered face detectors of the time in terms of computational efficiency and detection rate, and it eventually became a popular algorithm used in consumer cameras.

concepts.title: End-to-end learning and the ImageNet Moment
concepts.one_liner: End-to-end learning replaces manual pipelines with a single system that learns every processing stage from input pixels to output predictions.
concepts.content: End-to-end learning refers to a system where each processing stage, from the input pixels to the output predictions, is handled by learned modules rather than a manual pipeline. This event, known as the "ImageNet Moment," was a watershed for learning-based vision. concepts.title: Learning as a search for mapping
concepts.one_liner: Learning-based vision treats the development of vision algorithms as an automated search for the mapping between input and output.
concepts.content: Learning-based vision is similar to traditional approaches in that it studies the structure of input, the structure of output, and the mapping between the two. The primary difference is how that mapping is found. In this sense, learners act as a new kind of vision scientist, playing the same role as humans who previously determined how vision works through deep thought. While machine learners often arrive at similar algorithms as those designed by humans, they are more powerful and have far exceeded human-designed algorithms in raw performance.

concepts.title: Future Directions in Vision Theories
concepts.one_liner: Future vision theories may address currently missing elements like visual common sense, multi-perceptual integration, and embodied perception.
concepts.content: From ancient Greek extramission theories to modern neural mechanisms and computer vision, our understanding of perception has evolved significantly. concepts.title: Extramission theory
concepts.one_liner: Extramission theory posits that vision occurs because the eye emits rays, like fingers sensing the world, composed of internal fire.
concepts.content:
Extramission theory, originating with Empedocles and followed by Plato and Euclid, provided one of the first theories of vision. Empedocles introduced the idea that all things are composed of four elements: fire, earth, air, and water. He claimed the eye contained these elements and that fire was responsible for creating rays that emanated from the eyes, functioning like fingers that sensed the world. This theory explained why some eyes, particularly those of cats, appeared to shine at night; it was assumed they contained so much fire that it became visible. While we now know this shine is reflected light, the theory was a logical attempt to explain vision without a modern understanding of light and reflection.

[FIGURE:5c6343e2e1c26338 | The extramission theory attributed the glow observed in cat eyes to the presence of fire inside them.]

concepts.recap_md: - Vision is caused by rays of fire emanating from the eye to sense the external world.

concepts.title: Plato's theory of vision
concepts.one_liner: Plato proposed that vision results from the coalescence of internal fire flowing from the eye with external light from the environment.
concepts.content: Plato's theory of vision combined elements of both intromission and extramission. He described the eyes as organs contrived to give light, where a pure, internal fire flows through the eye in a smooth, dense stream. When the light of day surrounds this stream of vision, the internal and external light coalesce to form a single body along the line of vision. This combined stream diffuses the motions of whatever it touches back to the soul, creating the perception of sight. At night, the stream of vision is cut off and extinguished because the external fire is absent. Plato notably considered vision less reliable than touch because it could only sense the side of an object facing the observer.

concepts.recap_md: - Sight occurs when internal fire from the eye meets and merges with external daylight.

When the light of day surrounds the stream of vision, then like falls upon like, and they coalesce, and one body is formed by natural affinity in the line of vision, wherever the light that falls from within meets with an external object.

concepts.title: Aristotle's critique of extramission
concepts.one_liner: Aristotle critiqued extramission by arguing that the eyes lack internal fire and that rays could not possibly reach distant stars.
concepts.content: Aristotle was critical of the extramission theory, pointing out that stars were too far away for rays from the eyes to reach them. He suggested that only certain objects, such as fire, are light sources, while other objects merely reflect rays that hit the eyes. Aristotle also rejected the belief that the eye contained internal fire, arguing instead that the element of perception must be water, as vision requires a transparent medium.

concepts.title: Ibn al-Haytham's scientific method in optics
concepts.one_liner: Hasan Ibn al-Haytham transformed optics into a scientific discipline by demonstrating that light rays bounce off objects and enter the eye to create vision.
concepts.content:
In the late tenth century, Hasan Ibn al-Haytham's work transformed initial Greek theories into a true scientific discipline. Ibn al-Haytham (965–1040 AD), known as Alhacen in the Latin world, published the Book of Optics between 1028 and 1038, a work considered by many to be the beginning of the scientific method. In this book, Ibn al-Haytham describes how light rays bounce off objects in all directions and that the rays only become visible when they reach the eye perpendicularly. He described the pinhole camera and invented the camera obscura.

(see figure: Alhacen's diagram of the eyes and the optic nerve (), drawn around the year 1027. It is one of the first drawings of the visual system. *Source*: MS Fatih 3212, vol. 1, fol. 81b, Süleimaniye Mosque...)

Ibn al-Haytham rejected the extramission theory, arguing that sight could be explained by light rays emitted by objects rather than rays emitted by the eye. His work built upon Ptolemy, Euclid, Galen, and Aristotle. While Ptolemy believed distance could be measured by a single eye feeling the length of a light ray, Ibn al-Haytham showed experimentally that both eyes were needed to perceive depth.
concepts.motivation_md: Ibn al-Haytham sought to replace speculative Greek theories of vision with an experimental framework, establishing the modern understanding that vision is the result of external light entering the eye.

He argued that sight could be explained by the light rays emitted by objects and that it was not necessary to assume that the eye emitted rays.

concepts.title: Perception as inference
concepts.one_liner: Perception is the process by which the mind finds the most likely representation of an object to explain sensory input.
concepts.content: Helmholtz was an important theorist in visual perception. He proposed that the general rule determining the ideas of vision is that objects are imagined as being present in the field of vision as would have to be there in order to produce the same impression on the nervous mechanism under ordinary conditions. Thus, the mind makes perceptions out of sensations, finding representations of the object most likely to explain the sensory input. This viewpoint relates to Bayesian methods for computer vision inference.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why vision is not just a passive recording of light, but an active mental construction that attempts to make sense of ambiguous sensory data.

concepts.title: Unconscious inference
concepts.one_liner: Perception involves unconscious conclusions where the brain interprets sensory responses to infer the state of the world.
concepts.content: Psychic acts of ordinary perception can be viewed as unconscious conclusions, distinguishing them from common conscious conclusions. For example, while an astronomer computing star positions based on observations is making a conscious conclusion, seeing light when pressing on the eye is an unconscious conclusion about the world based on the eye's response. This concept of unconscious inference is a foundational topic in computer vision.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains that perception is not just a direct recording of the world but an active, inferential process. It provides a theoretical bridge between human psychology and the computational tasks of computer vision.
concepts.recap_md:

 - It differs from conscious reasoning, such as mathematical computation or formal observation.
 - This inferential framework is a core principle in the field of computer vision.

key_passage.text: Still, it may be permissible to speak of the psychic acts of ordinary perception as unconscious conclusions, thereby making a distinction of some sort between them and the common so-called conscious conclusions.

concepts.title: Active role of the viewer in perception
concepts.one_liner: Perception is an active process where viewers use their own movements to understand the stationary forms of objects.
concepts.content: Helmholtz emphasized the active role of the viewer in perception. He argued that if objects were simply passed before our eyes by a foreign force without our agency, we might never navigate the resulting optical phantasmagoria. By changing our position, we notice that we can obtain various images of an object, such as a table, at will. Through these movements, we discover that the stationary form of the object in space is the cause of the changing images in our eyes. This perspective foreshadows certain unsupervised learning methods used in modern computer vision.
concepts.motivation_md: It explains how humans resolve visual ambiguity by interacting with the environment, suggesting that movement is key to learning the stable properties of objects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Viewers play an active role in perception through physical movement.
 - Movement allows the brain to link changing retinal images to stationary 3D forms.
 - This principle is a precursor to unsupervised learning in computer vision.

concepts.title: Gestalt theory: Wholes over parts
concepts.one_liner: Gestalt theory posits that perception is about experiencing wholes as single units rather than just a collection of constituent parts.
concepts.content: Gestalt theory postulates that perceived motion is a new phenomenon not present in individual stimuli, and that we perceive whole events as single units. Gestalt psychology emerged as a reaction to the trend that psychology must decompose stimuli into constituent elements to be a science. Instead, Gestalt theory argues that perception is about wholes more than it is about parts.
concepts.motivation_md: This theory addresses why we see coherent objects and scenes instead of a chaotic mess of individual pixels or features.
concepts.recap_md:
- Perception focuses on wholes rather than individual constituent parts.
 - Perceived phenomena (like motion) can exist in the whole even if absent in the parts.
 - It challenges the reductionist view of psychology.

concepts.title: Perceptual organization
concepts.one_liner: Perceptual organization is the study of how the visual system organizes individual features into coherent objects and wholes.
concepts.content: Perceptual organization studies how our visual system organizes individual visual features, such as colors and lines, into coherent objects and wholes. This field explores the rules used by the visual system to group elements on a display. concepts.title: Center-Surround Organization
concepts.one_liner: Retinal ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with a circular center-surround organization that performs contrast enhancement.
concepts.content: Steven Kuffler demonstrated that retinal ganglion cells have concentric receptive fields with a circular center-surround organization. By recording the response of ganglion cells to small spots of light, he identified two primary types. On-center cells are activated when light falls within a small central region of the receptive field and are deactivated when light hits a surrounding ring. Off-center cells exhibit the opposite behavior. This organization suggests that the retina performs a contrast-enhancing operation, a discovery that has motivated extensive research in computational neuroscience and neuromorphic engineering. For his discoveries on how the eye processes visual information, Haldan Keffer Hartline received the Nobel Prize in 1967.
concepts.motivation_md: This organization allows the visual system to detect edges and changes in light intensity rather than just absolute light levels, effectively performing contrast enhancement at the very first stage of visual processing.

  "- This structure enables the retina to perform contrast enhancement and edge detection."
]

key_passage.text: He did this by shining a small spot of light on different parts of the retina and recording the response of a ganglion cell as he changed the location of the spot of light. First Hartline, and then Kuffler, showed that there were two types of ganglion cells; a first group of cells, called on-center, would get activated when the spot of light was inside a small region in the middle of the receptive field and would get deactivated (firing bellow their average rate) when the spot light was projected inside a ring around the center. A second group had the opposite behavior, called off-center.

concepts.title: Lateral Geniculate Nucleus (LGN)
concepts.one_liner: The lateral geniculate nucleus is a six-layered structure that relays visual signals from the retina to the cortex while receiving significant feedback.
concepts.content: The axons of ganglion cells from both eyes project to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), a structure composed of six layers of neurons that outputs to the visual cortex. Although it receives inputs from both eyes, the signals are not mixed, and the neurons remain monocular. LGN neurons possess concentric center-surround receptive fields. While its role is not fully understood, it may be involved in temporal decorrelation, attention modulation, and saccadic suppression. Interestingly, only 5 percent of the input connections come from the retina, while 95 percent are feedback connections from the primary visual cortex and other areas.
concepts.motivation_md: The LGN acts as a sophisticated relay station that filters and modulates visual information from the retina before it reaches the cortex, likely integrating top-down signals for attention and focus.

concepts.title: Oriented Simple Cell
concepts.one_liner: Oriented simple cells in the visual cortex increase their firing rate when stimulated by a bar of light at a specific orientation.

concepts.title: Organization of the Primary Visual Cortex (V1)
concepts.one_liner: The primary visual cortex is organized into functional columns and hypercolumns that process orientation, ocular dominance, and color.
concepts.content: The first visual area in the cortex, V1, is a sheet of neurons arranged in several layers. Hubel and Wiesel discovered that V1 neurons are organized into columns. Within a vertical column, all cells are selective to the same orientation. Moving horizontally, the preferred orientation changes smoothly (orientation columns), while moving perpendicularly reveals alternating eye preferences (ocular dominance columns). A hypercolumn, measuring approximately 1 $\times$ 3 mm, covers all orientations and both eyes for a small portion of the visual field. Additionally, color-sensitive neurons are organized in blobs surrounded by orientation-sensitive neurons.
concepts.motivation_md: This highly regular architecture ensures that every point in the visual field is systematically analyzed for all possible orientations and inputs from both eyes.

  "- V1 is organized into vertical columns where neurons share the same orientation preference.",

  "- Hypercolumns are functional units that process all orientations and both eyes for a small area of the visual field."
]

key_passage.text: Hubel and Wiesel found that neurons in V1 are organized along columns. When probing with an electrode, as the electrode went from the surface to the bottom of V1, all the cells found were selective to the same orientation. When moving the electrode along one horizontal direction, they found that the preferred orientation changed smoothly (orientation columns), and when moving the electrode along the perpendicular horizontal direction, the cells changed the eye preference, alternating between the two eyes with some binocular cells between them (ocular dominance columns).

concepts.title: Affordance
concepts.one_liner: An affordance is a property of an environment or object that offers an observer possibilities for action, such as a path affording locomotion.
concepts.content: Introduced by Gibson in 1966, an affordance is what an environment or object offers an observer. For example, a path affords locomotion, an obstacle affords collision, and a stairway affords both descent and ascent. An object's affordance is generally a direct consequence of its properties, such as a hollow object affording containment or a sharp edge affording cutting. Animate objects afford social interaction.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how we perceive the environment not just as physical shapes, but as opportunities for action, simplifying the link between perception and behavior.
concepts.recap_md: - Affordances are the action possibilities provided by the environment or objects to an observer. - These possibilities are often direct consequences of physical properties, such as a hollow object affording containment. - Animate objects are unique in that they afford social interaction.

concepts.title: Direct Perception
concepts.one_liner: Direct perception is the process of picking up information directly from a rich ambient optic array without the need for additional mental processing.
concepts.content: Gibson's theory of visual perception postulates that the ambient optic array is very rich and contains all the information needed to perceive the environment. Direct perception is the process of information pickup directly from this ambient array. This is in contrast with other theories of visual perception that assume input stimuli are impoverished and that perception is indirect, requiring additional processes. A richer input might allow for a simpler solution to the perception problem.
concepts.motivation_md: It challenges the idea that the brain must perform complex computations to 'fill in' missing data, suggesting instead that the environment provides sufficient information for immediate understanding.
concepts.recap_md: - Direct perception involves the immediate pickup of information from the ambient optic array. - It assumes the environment provides rich enough information that additional cognitive processing is unnecessary. - This approach suggests that richer sensory input can simplify the overall problem of perception.

concepts.title: Indirect Perception

concepts.title: Neural Mechanisms of Visual Perception

concepts.title: The Retina
concepts.one_liner: The retina is a neural structure that transforms light into electrical impulses and performs the initial stages of visual processing.
concepts.content: ![Drawing of the retina by Santiago Ramón y Cajal.](figures/taxonomy/cajal.png) The drawing of the retina (@fig-cajal) shows the first layers of neurons that process visual input. The retina transforms light into electrical impulses, starting with photoreceptors (rods and cones) and continuing through layers of amacrine, bipolar, and ganglion cells. Ganglion cells then transmit the output through the optic nerve to the rest of the brain. While Ramón y Cajal revealed this circuitry, his work did not fully explain the functional behavior of these circuits.
concepts.motivation_md: The retina acts as the primary transducer for vision, converting physical light into a language the brain can understand and performing initial data compression.
concepts.recap_md: - The retina transforms light into electrical signals using photoreceptors like rods and cones. - Information is processed through layers of amacrine, bipolar, and ganglion cells before leaving via the optic nerve. - It represents the first stage of neural circuitry in the visual processing stream.

concepts.title: Receptive Field
concepts.one_liner: A receptive field is the specific region of the input stimulus space that must be stimulated to produce a response in a particular neuron.
concepts.content: The retina was one of the first visual structures studied from a functional perspective. In 1938, Haldan Keffer Hartline popularized the concept of the receptive field, which corresponds to the region of the input stimulus space—the retina—that must be stimulated to produce a response in a neuron. Most neurons in the visual processing stream are activated only when light shines on a precise portion of the retina. Only stimulation within the receptive field (RF) produces a response. [FIGURE:542154188035b8df]
concepts.motivation_md: This concept allows researchers to map how specific neurons correspond to specific parts of the environment, explaining how the brain organizes spatial information.
concepts.recap_md: - A receptive field is the area of the sensory surface where a stimulus triggers a neuronal response. - Visual neurons typically respond only to light within a specific, precise portion of the retina. - This concept is fundamental to understanding how the visual system processes spatial information.

concepts.title: Gibson's Ecological Approach to Visual Perception
concepts.one_liner: Gibson's ecological approach to visual perception argues that vision should be studied in the context of the body and the environment.
concepts.content: James J. Gibson postulated that, to understand vision, one should take an ecological approach to visual perception. The study of the eye should be done in the context of the body that supports it and the world it lives in. Gibson argued that the experimental lab should be like real life, as simple stimuli are too limiting. The environment should be studied by means of ecological properties—understanding what quantities and processes are relevant for the observer—rather than just physical laws. An ecological description includes medium, substances, and surfaces, together with the notions of change and persistence. The ground plane is the most important surface for terrestrial animals, providing the support for action and a reference for perception. Other notions of ecological importance are the concepts of layout, place, and enclosure. [FIGURE:ec27a980e52fb1da]
concepts.motivation_md: Gibson sought to move perception research toward understanding how vision functions for survival and action in the real world rather than in artificial lab settings.
concepts.recap_md: - Perception is studied in the context of the observer's environment and bodily actions. - It prioritizes ecological properties like surfaces and substances over abstract physical laws.

concepts.title: The Structure of Ambient Light
concepts.one_liner: Ambient light is a complex pattern of light rays that fill a space through continuous interactions with surfaces before reaching an observer.
concepts.content: From a light source, a dense array of light rays emerges in all directions. Before these light rays reach the eye, the light interacts with the objects in the world. Consider a single ray emerging from the light source: if the light ray is not directed toward the eye, it will strike some surface in the world and, as result, a new set of rays will be emitted in many directions. This process continues, producing more interactions and filling the space. The observer senses only a subset of the light rays that strike the eye. As a result of this complex pattern of interactions, even a single ray will form a complex image in the eye of the observer. ![(a) Scene illuminated with a ceiling lamp. (b-c) Two images obtained by illuminating a scene with a laser pointer (the red line indicates the direction of the ray).](figures/taxonomy/lightGray2.png){#fig-lightRay} The resulting images show the complexity of the interactions between different surfaces. The sum of the contribution of all the light rays emitted by the light source will give rise to a natural looking picture. Despite the complexity of the structure of the ambient light (a term coined by James J. Gibson @Gibson1966) with multiple reflections, shadows, and specular surfaces, our visual system has no problem in interacting with this scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the structure of ambient light is crucial because it represents the raw input that the visual system must process to perceive the environment.
concepts.recap_md: - Ambient light consists of a dense array of rays interacting with surfaces in a space. - The visual system interprets complex patterns of reflections and shadows to perceive a coherent scene.

concepts.title: Plenoptic Function
concepts.one_liner: The plenoptic function $P (\theta, \Phi, \lambda, t, X, Y, Z)$ describes the light intensity of every ray in a space across position, direction, wavelength, and time.
concepts.content: The pattern of light filling the space can be described by the function: $$P (\theta, \Phi, \lambda, t, X, Y, Z)$$ where $P$ is the light intensity of a ray passing by the world location $(X,Y,Z)$ in the direction given by the angle $(\theta, \Phi)$, and with wavelength $\lambda$ at an instant in time $t$. This function, called the plenoptic function by Edward H. Adelson and James R. Bergen @Adelson91, contains all the information needed to describe the complete pattern of light rays that fills the space. Adelson originally considered calling it the holoscopic function.
concepts.motivation_md: The plenoptic function provides a formal mathematical representation of all available visual information in a scene, serving as the theoretical basis for image capture and analysis.
concepts.recap_md: - The plenoptic function captures light intensity as a function of position, direction, wavelength, and time. - It represents the totality of light rays available to an observer in a given environment.

concepts.title: Occlusion in Vision
concepts.one_liner: Occlusion occurs when surfaces are hidden from an observer, presenting a significant challenge for the visual system to interpret hidden parts of a scene.
concepts.content: For a given observer, most of the light rays are occluded. Without occlusion, vision would be a lot simpler. Occlusion is the best example of how hard vision can get. Many times, properly interpreting an image will require understanding what part is occluded (e.g., we know that a person is not floating just because the legs are occluded behind a table). Unfortunately, occlusions are common. In fact, there are more occluded surfaces than visible surfaces for any given observer.
concepts.motivation_md: Occlusion is a fundamental problem in vision because it results in missing information that the brain must infer to maintain a consistent understanding of the world.
concepts.recap_md: - Occlusion is the phenomenon where objects or surfaces block the view of other surfaces. - Interpreting scenes requires the visual system to infer the existence and properties of hidden objects.

concepts.title: Visual Awareness
concepts.one_liner: Visual awareness is the subjective experience of vision, influenced by internal states, knowledge, and expectations rather than just external input.
concepts.content: Vision is not a deterministic process that analyzes the input images independently of our internal state. concepts.title: Vision as Extracting Scene Properties
concepts.one_liner: The goal of vision is to extract meaningful scene properties like surfaces and objects from light patterns, rather than just measuring light intensities.

concepts.title: Intromission theory
concepts.one_liner: Early intromission theory proposed that objects emit physical copies of themselves, called eidola or simulacra, which enter the eyes to create vision.
concepts.content: Early intromission theories (425 BC) believed that objects emitted copies of themselves (eidola or simulacra) that entered the eyes. This theory was defended by philosophers such as Demokritos, Epicurus, and Lucretius. However, it was unclear how objects could be sending copies when there were multiple observers, and how the copies did not interfere with each other. It was also unclear how copies of large objects could fit into the eye.
concepts.motivation_md: This historical theory represents an early attempt to explain the physical mechanism of sight before the modern understanding of light and optics.

concepts.title: Marr's Computational Theory of Vision (Introduction)
concepts.one_liner: David Marr's philosophy of vision treats perception as an information-processing task influenced by computer vision, cognitive psychology, and neurophysiology.
concepts.content: David Marr's influential book *Vision* was published posthumously in 1982. Marr's philosophy was influenced by advances in computer vision, and studies in cognitive psychology and neurophysiology. Studies in psychology at the time suggested that visual information was processed by independent modules of perception, each one devoted to a specific task (stereo vision, motion perception, color processing), and that visual images were analyzed by independent spatial-frequency-tuned channels. Progress in neurophysiological experiments using single cell recordings showed a strong connection between perception and neural activity. In the 1970s, computer vision was already a well-established field. Some of the advances that inspired Marr's philosophy were the work by David L. Waltz on the interpretation of block worlds, Edwin H. Land and John J. McCann's Retinex theory about color perception, and Berthold Horn's theory of shape from shading, among many other works.
concepts.motivation_md: Marr sought to provide a rigorous framework for vision by integrating psychology, neuroscience, and computer science into a unified information-processing perspective.
concepts.recap_md: - Vision is viewed as an information-processing task involving independent modules for specific tasks like motion or color. - The theory integrates insights from neurophysiology, cognitive psychology, and early computer vision research.

concepts.title: Marr's Three Levels of Description
concepts.one_liner: David Marr proposed that information-processing systems like vision should be understood at three levels: computational theory, representation, and hardware.
concepts.content: David Marr, together with Tomaso Poggio and others, postulated that it was important to separate the analysis of the task being solved from the particular mechanism used to solve it. Marr said that the vision problem should be understood at different levels, and that what was missing in previous theories of vision was to understand vision as an **information-processing task**. Marr proposed that an information-processing device should be described at three levels: (1) **Computational theory**: This level of description should answer what the task is to be performed and why it should be carried out. In the case of vision, the task is to derive properties of the world from images. This level specifies the mapping between input and output and why it is appropriate, without specifying the algorithm. (2) **Representation**: This defines the system used for the input and output. The choice of representation (e.g., pixel values vs. Fourier decomposition) makes certain information explicit while hiding other information, which heavily influences the algorithm's performance. (3) **Hardware**: Finally, the representation and algorithm must be implemented in a physical device. Marr noted that explaining visual phenomena requires finding the right level of description. For instance, the trichromatic color theory is explained by the hardware level, while the bistable nature of the Necker cube is likely related to the 3D representation. Illusions, such as those in @fig-measuringScene, are also likely due to the representation and algorithm used rather than the hardware. Marr considered that Gibson was asking the right questions but had a naive view of the difficulty of solving them.
concepts.motivation_md: This framework allows researchers to study the "what" and "why" of vision independently of the biological or mechanical "how," preventing confusion between task goals and implementation.
concepts.recap_md: - The computational level defines the task goals and the logic of the transformation. - The representation level specifies the data structures and algorithms used to process information. - The hardware level describes the physical realization of the system, such as neurons or silicon chips.

slots.example: David Marr, together with Tomaso Poggio and others, postulated that it was important to separate the analysis of the task being solved from the particular mechanism used to solve it. Marr said that the vision problem should be understood at different levels, and that what was missing in previous theories of vision was to understand vision as an **information-processing task**. Marr proposed that an information-processing device should be described at three levels: (1) **Computational theory**: This level of description should answer what the task is to be performed and why it should be carried out. In the case of vision, the task is to derive properties of the world from images. This level specifies the mapping between input and output and why it is appropriate, without specifying the algorithm. (2) **Representation**: This defines the system used for the input and output. The choice of representation (e.g., pixel values vs. Fourier decomposition) makes certain information explicit while hiding other information, which heavily influences the algorithm's performance. (3) **Hardware**: Finally, the representation and algorithm must be implemented in a physical device. Marr noted that explaining visual phenomena requires finding the right level of description. For instance, the trichromatic color theory is explained by the hardware level, while the bistable nature of the Necker cube is likely related to the 3D representation. Illusions, such as those in @fig-measuringScene, are also likely due to the representation and algorithm used rather than the hardware. Marr considered that Gibson was asking the right questions but had a naive view of the difficulty of solving them.

concepts.title: Computational Theory (Marr's Level 1)
concepts.one_liner: The computational theory level defines the specific task an information-processing device performs and the logic behind why that task is necessary.
concepts.content: **Computational theory**. This level of description should answer the following questions: what is the task to be performed and why should it be carried out? In the case of vision, the task is to derive properties of the world from images. This level of description should specify what the mapping is between the input and output, and why this mapping is appropriate for the task that the device needs to solve. This level does not specify how that mapping should be constructed or which algorithm will implement it.
concepts.motivation_md: It establishes the fundamental goals and constraints of a system, ensuring we understand the problem before attempting to design a specific solution or algorithm.
concepts.recap_md: - Identifies the goal of the computation and the logic of the strategy used to carry it out. - Focuses on the "what" and "why" rather than the "how."

concepts.title: Representation (Marr's Level 2)
concepts.one_liner: The representation level defines the data structures and algorithms used to transform input into output, determining which information is made explicit.
concepts.content: **Representation**. We should define which representation will be used for the input and output. The representation is a system of making explicit certain types of information present on a signal. For instance, an image could be represented by the sequence of values that encode the color of each pixel, but it could be also represented using a Fourier decomposition. The choice of representation will make explicit certain type of information while hiding other information, which will become harder to access. The algorithm used to implement the mapping between input and output will be strongly dependent on the representation used. Examples such as using position encoding to represent location illustrate the dramatic effect that the choice of representation and algorithm can have in the final system performance.
concepts.motivation_md: Different representations make different features of the data accessible; choosing the right one is essential for the efficiency and success of the subsequent processing algorithms.
concepts.recap_md: - Specifies the formal system for representing input and output information. - Determines the efficiency and nature of the algorithm used to process the data.

concepts.title: Hardware (Marr's Level 3)
concepts.one_liner: The hardware level describes the physical implementation of the representation and algorithm in a biological or mechanical device.
concepts.content: **Hardware**. Finally, the representation and algorithm will have to be implemented in a physical device. Marr noted that when trying to explain visual phenomena, one needs to find what is the right level to use to describe it. For instance, the trichromatic color theory of human perception is explained by the hardware level (i.e., by the three color receptors in our retina) while the bistable nature of the Necker cube is likely to be related to the 3D representation. The illusions shown in @fig-measuringScene, are also likely due to the representation and algorithm used and they are rather independent on the particular hardware implementation. Marr considered that Gibson was asking the right questions, getting very close to a computational theory of vision, but that he had a naive view on how difficult it would be to solve them.

concepts.title: Primal Sketch
concepts.one_liner: The primal sketch represents fundamental changes in an image, such as edges and junctions, along with their spatial organization.
concepts.content: Primal sketch: Represents changes in the image (edges, junctions, zero-crossings) and their spatial organization.
concepts.motivation_md: It serves as the first stage of visual processing, converting raw pixel intensities into a more useful map of basic geometric features.
concepts.recap_md: - Captures basic image features like edges and junctions. - Organizes these features spatially to provide a foundation for further processing.

concepts.title: 2.5D Sketch (Depth Map)
concepts.one_liner: The 2.5D sketch, or depth map, estimates the distance to visible surfaces and identifies depth discontinuities and surface orientations.
concepts.content: 2.5D sketch: Contains an estimation of the distance between the observer and the visible surfaces in the world at each pixel, also called a **depth map**. It also contains information about depth discontinuities and surface orientations.
concepts.motivation_md: It bridges the gap between 2D image features and 3D object models by representing the geometry of the scene from the observer's perspective.
concepts.recap_md: - Provides a pixel-wise estimation of distance (depth) from the observer. - Includes information on surface orientation and depth discontinuities.
